title: She loved much (Luke 7:36–50)
hookLine: a woman with a reputation washes his feet with her tears at a proud host's dinner
last: GO AND TELL WHAT YOU'VE SEEN.

cards: A dinner party at the house of a Pharisee named Simon. The guests recline on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow, feet stretched out behind them.
Some historians think dinners like this could be semi-public, with people from town standing at the edges to listen. One of them slips in. Luke calls her "a woman in the city, which was a sinner."

He never says what her sin was, and never gives her name. She carries an alabaster jar of perfumed oil, and stands behind Jesus, at his feet. And before she can do whatever she came to do, she starts to cry.

teach.b: In the King James words, she "began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment."
Simon thinks, but doesn't say: if this man were a prophet, he'd know what kind of woman this is.

teach.h: SIMON, I HAVE SOMEWHAT TO SAY.
teach.b: Jesus answers the thought: "Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee." And Simon, politely: "Master, say on." Jesus speaks to him by name, as his host, not as a villain.
Two people owe a moneylender, one five hundred coins, one fifty. Neither can pay, and he forgives them both. "Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?"
Simon: "I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most."
Then Jesus turns toward the woman, still talking to Simon: "Seest thou this woman?" Simon has seen a reputation. Jesus asks him to see a person.
You gave me no water for my feet; she washed them with tears. You gave me no kiss; she hasn't stopped kissing my feet. You didn't anoint my head; she anointed my feet.

teach.h: HER SINS, WHICH ARE MANY, ARE FORGIVEN; FOR SHE LOVED MUCH.
teach.b: "Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little." And to her: "Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace." She came in carrying a reputation.

how: Some Christians read this story when thinking about confession and forgiveness, and the woman's tears are often remembered as a picture of love and repentance.

games.q: you're the host. a woman everyone talks about is crying over your guest's feet. your guest turns to you. what does he say?
o: "Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee," and he tells a story about two debtors.
"don't worry, I'll speak to her later."
games.why: Jesus tells Simon a parable, asks him which debtor loves more, and then asks: seest thou this woman?

practice: Think of something you've done that still makes you wince, maybe already forgiven, by the person or by God, and never quite let in.

Picture yourself at that table in the woman's place and hear the words: not it didn't matter, just forgiven, go in peace. If you pray, you can hear them as spoken to you; if you don't, simply practice setting the weight down.

wordCard.voice: Agapao, the Greek word for love behind the phrase she loved much: an unnamed woman at a Pharisee's dinner washes Jesus' feet with her tears, and leaves forgiven, in peace.
